opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest way to put it is that the tabletop system and an action-grammar approach were trying to answer different questions, and each has a ceiling that shows up in different places.

An action-grammar approach is very appealing on paper. You decompose a task into primitives like reach, grasp, move, place, and then you have rules for composing them. It's interpretable, it generalizes compositionally in a clean way, and when the world matches your assumptions it can be quite robust. The problem is that the grammar is only as good as the vocabulary you hand-design. Real tabletop manipulation is full of in-between cases: a grasp that's also a push, an object that's partially occluded, a cup that's a bit tilted. Those don't fit neatly into a symbol. So the grammar ends up either very brittle or keeps growing more rules, and that doesn't scale.

What we tried to do in that first paper was let more of the structure come from perception and from data: understand the objects and their geometry well enough, in a category-level way, that the system can act on things it hasn't seen exactly before. What that bought us was generalization across object instances, which the grammar approach struggles with because it usually assumes you already know what and where the object is.

But I'd be careful not to oversell it. Within the tabletop setting, with a constrained set of tasks and objects, it could do things reliably that a hand-written grammar would find tedious. What it couldn't do was long-horizon reasoning, or really open-ended tasks where you need to plan many steps and recover from failure. There, honestly, some kind of structured or hierarchical representation, which is the spirit of action grammars, is still valuable.

So my view, looking back, is that it isn't one versus the other. The lesson was that the low-level, contact-rich, geometry-heavy part should be learned and grounded in perception, because that's where hand design fails. The high-level composition can benefit from structure, and today a lot of that role is played by language models rather than hand-built grammars. That first paper was one step toward the grounded half of that picture, not the whole answer.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back at that first paper honestly, I'd say the tabletop system did something narrower than what it looked like it was doing. What it could actually achieve was mapping a fairly constrained set of instructions onto pick-and-place behaviors in a scene where the objects, the workspace, and the vocabulary were all pre-defined. Within that envelope it was quite robust. Outside of it, it fell apart in ways that weren't always graceful, and that's the part people didn't see in the videos.

The action-grammar approach starts from a different premise. Instead of learning a direct mapping from perception to a flat action, you impose a compositional structure: primitives, operators that combine them, and rules about which combinations are valid. The appeal is that you get generalization almost for free in a certain sense. If the system knows "grasp," "move-above," and "release," and knows how to sequence them, it can in principle produce a stacking behavior it was never explicitly shown.

So on the axis of combinatorial generalization, the grammar approach is clearly stronger, and I think our tabletop system would lose that comparison. But there's a cost people underweight. The grammar has to be designed by someone, and every design decision bakes in assumptions about what the task space looks like. When a new object shape or a slightly different contact situation shows up, the grammar either has a rule for it or it doesn't. Our end-to-end system, for all its brittleness, could sometimes absorb that kind of variation because it wasn't committed to a symbolic carving of the world.

Where I've landed is that neither one was right, and the interesting work since then has been about getting the compositional structure to emerge from data rather than specifying it by hand, and letting perception stay continuous underneath it. If I were to redo that first paper, I wouldn't choose between them. I'd ask what minimum amount of structure you need to inject so that learning does the rest.

astra-6.text: I’d distinguish between completing a particular tabletop task and having a general way to compose actions. The system in our first paper was a demonstration of what we could achieve in that setting; I wouldn’t take success there as evidence that it could handle arbitrary combinations of tasks. An action-grammar approach makes the structure explicit—how simpler actions can be combined into more complex sequences. That offers a route to reuse and composition, but the grammar alone doesn’t solve the problem of grounding those actions in perception and executing them reliably. So the comparison is partly about demonstrated task performance and partly about the scope for generalization.

sol-6.1.text: I’d distinguish between demonstrating a set of tabletop skills and having a general way to compose those skills. Our first system could address the tasks we studied, but that alone wouldn’t establish that it could handle new combinations or longer sequences. An action-grammar approach offers a structure for composing actions, which could make that kind of generalization easier. But the grammar still needs reliable perception and execution underneath it. So I’d compare them on whether they can complete unfamiliar tasks, how much task-specific design they require, and how well they recover when something goes wrong.
